title: Social Media Use, Fake News and Mental Health during the Uncertain Times of the COVID-19 Pandemic in Ukraine
screen_reason: Online survey of Ukrainian social-media users reporting the share of respondents who observed COVID-19 fake news going viral in their city: 58.8% (118/199) in the first wave and 39.6% (60/152) in the second. That is a share of survey respondents who say they encountered misinformation, i.e. RECALL (exposure). The study's aim is mental health, but the descriptive share is reported in the abstract, the results text and Table 3.

estimates.platform: social media, chiefly Facebook and Instagram (self-report in an online survey)
estimates.date: first wave: 15 March - 25 April 2020 (second wave: 10 October - 25 November 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who reported observing COVID-19 fake news that went viral in their city
estimates.value_raw: First wave: Yes 118 (58.8%), No 81 (41.2%) of n = 199 (Table 3). Second wave: Yes 60 (39.6%), No 92 (60.4%) of n = 152
estimates.denominator: 199 Ukrainian adults (18-60, using social media for at least six months) who completed the online survey in the first wave, 15 March - 25 April 2020
estimates.definition: answered 'Yes' to observing fake news related to COVID-19 going viral in their own city
estimates.misinfo_def: No definition was given to respondents. The paper's own framing: "the observation of fake news related to COVID-19 going viral in the participants' respective cities"; elsewhere "the Internet may lead to the dissemination of unverified or unreported information".
estimates.source_quote: As indicated in Table 3, the observation of fake news related to COVID-19 going viral in the participants’ respective cities was reported by 58.8% (n = 118 out of 199) of the participants from the first survey and decreased in the second survey, with only 39.6% (n = 60 out of 152) of respondents noting them (chi-square, p = 0.0001 vs. first survey).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single yes/no self-report item in a Google Forms survey; 'fake news' was never defined for participants, no examples were offered, and no time window is stated for the observation. Respondents judged both the falsity and the virality themselves.
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were Ukrainian individuals using social media for at least six months.
estimates.notes: TIME-SERIES COLLAPSE: the paper reports the same item in two independent survey waves (58.8% of 199 in wave 1; 39.6% of 152 in wave 2, chi-square p = 0.0002 per Table 3 / p = 0.0001 per the text). I entered the FIRST WAVE as the representative point because it is the abstract's headline figure ('the observation of fake news that went viral (58.8%)') and covers the peak-uncertainty period; the second-wave value is recorded verbatim in value_raw so an adjudicator can add it as a second row if the project prefers per-wave rows. A pooled figure is not entered because (118+60)/351 would be a cross-category sum, which R8 forbids. ARITHMETIC FLAG: Table 3's first-wave cells are internally inconsistent - 118/199 is 59.3% and 81/199 is 40.7%, whereas the stated 58.8%/41.2% correspond to 117/82. The percentage was entered as printed. SAMPLE: a snowball convenience sample recruited through social media, heavily skewed to young women (81.2%) and students (42.9%), all born in the early 1990s, and 78.6% preferring social media over traditional news - so this is not a general-population prevalence for Ukraine. No response rate can be computed for a snowball design. Also note the item measures PERCEIVED presence of viral fake news in the respondent's environment, which the review's criteria admit, rather than personal exposure to a specific false claim.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) No second row for wave 2 - see the entered row's notes (time-series collapse; value recorded there). (2) 'Overall, when the two surveys were taken into account, the daily use of social media was reported by 43.7% (n = 153 out of 350) as increasing after the first COVID-19-positive case was reported' and '24.9% (n = 87 out of 350) of participants browsed Facebook and Instagram more frequently in the previous month to find news and information about COVID-19' - social media USE and information seeking, not misinformation exposure, so no rows. Note the denominator slips from 351 to 350 in these two sentences without explanation. (3) 'Out of 351 respondents, 275 (78.6%) preferred to follow news from social media rather than traditional media' - news preference, not misinformation. (4) Time-use figures (3.18 h/day on social media, 1.01 h/day on COVID-19 content in wave 1; 31.9% of social-media time spent on COVID-19 content in wave 1 vs 19.45% in wave 2) are exposure to COVID-19 CONTENT generally, not to misinformation, so they are not per-capita misinformation intensity rows. (5) All mental-health outcomes (PSS-10 total 20.61, GAD-7 total 14.17, severe anxiety 8.5% vs 3.3%, sleep alteration 46.7%, appetite change 32.7%, 34.2% reporting deteriorated well-being) are outcomes, not misinformation measures. (6) 'videos with misleading content sometimes garnered 75% more views than those from credible sources [8]' and 'The majority of participants watched fake news spread on Facebook [17]' in the introduction/discussion are figures cited from other papers - excluded by R8. (7) The GAD-7 total scores (14.17, 13.62) are inconsistent with the paper's own interpretation of them as 'mild anxiety' (the stated mild band is 5-9 and 14-21 would be moderate-to-severe), and Table 5's severe-anxiety cell is printed as '>17 (8.5%)'. These do not affect the extracted row but show the paper's numerical reporting is unreliable in places - relevant to risk-of-bias weighting. (8) No behavioural, content or concentration data anywhere in the study: it is survey-only.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey in two waves during the COVID-19 pandemic in Ukraine: wave 1 15 March - 25 April 2020 (n = 199), wave 2 10 October - 25 November 2020 (n = 152), total n = 351 adults aged 18-60 who had used social media for at least six months. Recruitment was by snowball sampling through social media using a Google Forms instrument, with electronic informed consent; the resulting sample is a convenience sample dominated by women (81.2%), students (42.9%) and Instagram users (60.3%), all Generation Z / born in the early 1990s, so no response rate or sampling frame can be established and the two waves are independent samples with significantly different age and occupation composition (wave 2 younger, more students), which confounds the wave-to-wave comparison. Misinformation exposure was measured with a single undefined self-report item about fake news going viral in the respondent's city; validated instruments (PSS-10, GAD-7) were used for the mental-health outcomes. Analysis: Student and paired t-tests, chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, GraphPad; no adjustment for multiple comparisons and no multivariable modelling. Several internal arithmetic inconsistencies (Table 3 counts vs percentages; denominators of 350 vs 351; GAD-7 band interpretation) reduce confidence in the reporting.
